# Grid Traversal and Data Structure Adaptation
## Overview
This family encompasses methods that adapt the domain traversal and data structures of isosurface extraction to handle sparse, hierarchical, or multi-resolution volumetric data, avoiding the memory and computational costs of dense regular grids [G]. Unlike standard grid-based methods that iterate over fixed arrays, these techniques traverse octrees, sparse point sets, or adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) boundaries, dynamically gathering scalar values and generating geometry only where necessary [G]. They are distinguished from their siblings by their specific approach to handling topological discontinuities: [Marching Cubes with Octree](1259-marching-cubes-with-octree.md) relies on uniform node sizing to prevent cracks, [Sparse Marching Cubes](3825-sparse-marching-cubes.md) uses dynamic lookup for scattered points, [Hierarchical Marching Cubes Enumeration](5223-hierarchical-marching-cubes-enumeration.md) explicitly separates traversal logic for faces, edges, and vertices to ensure coherence, and [2D Stitching](10249-2d-stitching.md) generates stitch cells to bridge AMR level gaps without subdividing quadrilaterals [G].
## Shared principles
Builds on the shared principles of [Grid Traversal and Data Structures](10325-grid-traversal-and-data-structures.md) [G].
## Subtopics

### [Marching Cubes with Octree](1259-marching-cubes-with-octree.md)
Applies the Marching Cubes algorithm over an octree data structure to convert volumetric scalar fields into triangle meshes. It solves the problem of efficiently processing sparse or unbounded datasets by replacing fixed-grid storage with a hierarchical structure, avoiding the iteration overhead of dense arrays. Unlike standard grid-based marching cubes, it adapts the domain traversal to the octree topology, though it requires uniform node sizes around the isosurface to prevent topological cracks. Choose this method when the data is naturally hierarchical and uniform refinement around the surface is feasible.

### [Sparse Marching Cubes](3825-sparse-marching-cubes.md)
Generates a triangle mesh from a sparse set of 3D points with associated scalar values (e.g., Signed Distance Fields), avoiding the memory overhead of dense 3D grids. It differs from standard Marching Cubes by dynamically gathering corner values for active voxels via lookup, rather than iterating over a fixed dense volume. Choose this method when the input is a sparse point cloud or SDF rather than a dense voxel grid.

### [Hierarchical Marching Cubes Enumeration](5223-hierarchical-marching-cubes-enumeration.md)
A recursive octree traversal algorithm that extracts isosurface meshes by enumerating voxel faces, edges, and vertices, delegating the actual geometry generation to a standard Marching Cubes routine at leaf nodes. It differs from [Marching Cubes with Octree](1259-marching-cubes-with-octree.md) and [Sparse Marching Cubes](3825-sparse-marching-cubes.md) by explicitly separating the traversal logic into specialized functions for faces, edges, and vertices to ensure coherent mesh generation across hierarchical boundaries. Choose this method when topological consistency across varying octree depths is critical.

### [2D Stitching](10249-2d-stitching.md)
An index-based tessellation scheme that fills topological gaps between dual grids of different Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) levels to generate crack-free isosurfaces. It merges coarse and fine grid levels seamlessly by generating "stitch cells" (triangles and deformed quadrilaterals) without subdividing existing boundary elements. Unlike constrained Delaunay triangulation, which requires subdividing quadrilateral boundary faces into triangles (causing cracks in 3D Marching Cubes extraction), this method preserves the quadrilateral topology of the grid boundaries. Choose this method when working with AMR grids that require crack-free transitions between refinement levels.

## Background
The need for adaptive grid traversal arises from the limitations of dense regular grids when handling large-scale, sparse, or multi-resolution data [G]. Early isosurface extraction methods assumed a uniform grid, leading to prohibitive memory usage for sparse fields [G]. Subsequent developments optimized traversal for non-uniform data distributions and AMR boundaries [G].
